newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian oil price rise unlikely until after budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian oil price rise unlikely until after budget.

text.p: The Indian government is unlikely to approve another increase in petroleum prices, a move it says is inevitable, until the national budget is handed down at the end of February, oil analysts said on Thursday.
Government ministers in the past have hinted at an oil price increase but gave no indication when it would come.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition government triggered an uproar last year when it announced sweeping oil price increases shortly after taking power in early July.

On Tuesday, Petroleum Minister T.R. Baalu said the oil pool subsidy bill was expected to reach a staggering 200 billion rupees ($5.5 billion) for 1996/97 (April-March), up from the earlier projection of 150 billion rupees.
"The minister seems to be revising the figure every morning," an oil analyst said. The oil pool account deficit has been revised upwards several times in the past six months.
Last week, the Economic Times newspaper said the government had initiated discussions with the Communist Party, a key backer of the United Front government, on a price hike.
The Communist Party is opposed to any hike.

Most analysts said the price hike would be part of the new budget proposals. One analyst said he expected a "soft budget", devoid of any price increases. But this would be followed by a rise in the prices of state-controlled commodities in the weaks after, he predicted. The budget is due by end February.

The Indian Express newspaper said on Thursday the government on Wednesday approved a proposal to raise the price paid to state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd for domestic crude oil.

In turn, these firms would pay higher royalty to states for onland oil production and to the federal government for onshore production, the newspaper said. It said the proposed hike in petroleum price looked imminent after this decision.
The Press Trust of India said, under the proposal, royalty rates would increase to 578 rupees a tonne from 528 rupees.
"A hike of 10 percent in petrol and 20 percent in diesel should raise 65 billion rupees," said an oil analyst. He said it would be difficult for the government to raise prices beyond this level.
The increases on these two products could be softened if the government chose to raise prices of other goods like naphtha.
Analysts attribute the sharp rise in oil pool account deficit to a fall in production of indigenous crude oil and a sharp rise in international crude prices.

ONGC, which accounts for about 90 percent of India's oil production, is expected to produce a little over 27 million tonnes in the year ending March 1997, down from about 31 million tonnes in the year-ago period.
A sharp rise in crude prices this year added to the oil pool deficit, analysts said.
Petroleum minister Baalu told a global oil conference in Goa last November that India's oil import bill for 1996/97 would rise to $9 billion from the earlier estimated $7.8 billion.

India imported over 22 million tonnes of crude and 16 million tonnes of refined products costing $6.5 billion in 1995/96. This accounted for 20-22 percent of the country's total import bill, according to official figures.
